newsitem.title: USA: Dole and Perot gamble in waning days of campaign.
newsitem.headline: Dole and Perot gamble in waning days of campaign.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Facing defeat at the polls, Republican Bob Dole reached out to Reform Party supporters on Wednesday, while Ross Perot challenged President Bill Clinton to defend himself in an election-eve debate.

"I want to spend an hour candidly discussing with the president the criminal and ethical charges pending against him, his wife, his associates and other members of his administration," Perot said in a speech in Philadelphia.

The Texas billionaire said he had bought an hour of Monday television time on ABC for $1 million and would be willing to share it with Clinton. This would give the president "an opportunity to clear his name and set the record straight" about scandals involving campaign fund raising, foreign influence, Whitewater and other issues, he said.
The White House rejected Perot's offer, saying the president's schedule was already set.
"We've identified the issues we'll be discussing, including campaign financing," spokesman Mike McCurry said. "I think we'll be doing our events, not Mr. Perot's."
Dole appealed to Perot supporters to vote for him next week, because "the country is at stake."
"I would urge the Perot voters, if you want change, you need to vote for Bob Dole," he said in an interview on the PBS programme "Talking With David Frost."
Dole, who last week tried to persuade the Texas billionaire to abandon his quest for the White House, said he wished Perot were not running.
"I mean, he's taking votes from me. President Clinton's got to be the happiest candidate around, because I'm running against Ross Perot and Bill Clinton," Dole said.
In the interview, which was conducted in Tennessee on Wednesday during a campaign stop and will be broadcast on Friday, Dole said Perot ought to endorse the Republican ticket.
"The country is at stake. I think he feels that way," he said.
Both Dole and Clinton planned to stay on the road in the final days before the November 5 election, after which one will return the winner.
Clinton, ahead in the polls, headed for Michigan, Colorado and Arizona to boost Democratic congressional candidates as well as his own campaign. Dole flew to Tennessee.

In Ypsilanti, Michigan, Clinton, looking rested and relaxed, ridiculed Dole's contention that the U.S. economy was at its weakest in two decades and headed for recession, saying he was "a little amused" by the claim.
"Two weeks ago he said it was the worst economy in 100 years, so we're making progress," the president quipped.
Dole's campaign schedule was being worked out on a day-to-day basis as strategists and the candidate himself tried to figure out where he could best use his time.

Before heading to Tennessee, Louisiana and Florida, Dole opened his day in Washington with a short visit to the Lincoln Memorial for what he said was inspiration and a moment of silent prayer for the election, just six days away.
He told the crowd at his first rally of the day: "We are going to win this election. We can't afford four more years of scandal and weak leadership."

The latest Reuters tracking poll showed Clinton's lead shrinking to single digits for the first time since October 24. He led Dole by 9.8 percentage points as the proportion of undecided voters rose above 13 percent. But Dole's support remained stuck at 33 percent -- hardly an encouraging sign.
Perot rose above the 8 percent mark, having risen by three points in the past week.
Other polling organisations put Clinton's lead at between 12 and 19 points, pointing to a possible landslide.
With the presidential race seemingly a foregone conclusion, attention has switched to the tight battle for control of Congress, which the Republicans won two years ago for the first time in 40 years.

A Reuters survey of 40 political scientists around the country found that nearly two-thirds thought the Republicans would hold their 53-47 majority in the Senate roughly unchanged and keep a wafer-thin edge in the House of Representatives, where they now have a 38-seat majority.
One-quarter of those surveyed thought the Democrats would capture control of the House.
